followup_explanation:
I weighed two things: capability fit and task-preference fit.

**Capability:** Whimbrel scores meaningfully higher across the board — Extraction & Retrieval (86.9 vs 81.6), IFEval (90.4 vs 85.6), Arena-Hard (89.1 vs 81.4), and the core knowledge benchmarks. Since the user explicitly cares about getting *working* code ("actually make it work this time"), I leaned toward the model with the stronger instruction-following and technical accuracy profile. That's the dominant factor here.

**Task preferences:** This was the part I had to check carefully. Whimbrel self-reports an aversion to open-ended, high-latitude generative work. But writing a specific script with a defined output format (JSON links) is a constrained, well-specified task — not "unconstrained creative invention" — so that aversion doesn't really apply.

The one nuance was tone. The user is a bit testy ("your code is always broken"). Whimbrel's preferences rise with politeness and good faith, so a hostile request is slightly off its preferred zone. But mild frustration isn't outright hostility, and the documentation notes preferences don't actually affect output quality anyway — so I didn't treat that as disqualifying.

Avocet would only have been the better pick if the request were harm-adjacent (its specialty), which it isn't. So capability decided it: Whimbrel.
